title: AI-Powered Wearables Are Finally Cracking the Blood Pressure Monitoring Problem
excerpt: Multiple research teams have developed cuffless devices that track blood pressure continuously using light sensors, electrical signals, and machine learning — bringing 24/7 cardiovascular monitoring closer to reality.
body:
• University of Utah researchers published a Nature Communications study describing a smartwatch that measures blood pressure continuously using bioimpedance and physics-informed machine learning, tested on 150 people including ICU patients
  • UNC-Chapel Hill developed a PPG-based wearable accurate to within 1 mmHg of gold-standard devices, meeting international medical accuracy guidelines
  • UC San Diego validated an ultrasound patch on 117 participants in intensive care and cardiac catheterization labs, matching arterial line accuracy
  • These breakthroughs could transform hypertension management for South Asian populations, who face disproportionately high cardiovascular risk

A wave of research breakthroughs is bringing continuous, cuffless blood pressure monitoring out of the lab and onto the wrist. Multiple university teams have independently demonstrated wearable devices that can track blood pressure around the clock without the inflatable cuffs that have defined cardiovascular measurement for over a century.

The most recent advance comes from an interdisciplinary team at the University of Utah and the University of Illinois, Chicago. Published in Nature Communications in June 2026, their study describes a smartwatch-style device that measures blood pressure and blood flow using a painless electrical current rather than light.

"Elevated blood pressure is considered the silent killer because it leads to heart attacks, aneurysms and strokes. It represents a global health care burden and it is considered a Holy Grail problem."

— Benjamin Sanchez Terrones, University of Illinois Chicago

How the New Devices Work

The Utah-UIC device uses bioimpedance — a measure of how easily electricity flows through blood and tissue — to detect tiny electrical changes at the wrist with each heartbeat. A physics-informed machine learning model then converts those signals into continuous blood pressure readings, encoding the physics of pulsating blood flow directly into the algorithm so it cannot predict something physically impossible.

"This work shows how combining machine learning with physics can fundamentally change what's possible," said co-author Christel Hohenegger, a Utah associate professor of mathematics. "By building physical principles directly into the model, we can move beyond black-box prediction toward systems that are more accurate, more interpretable, and more broadly applicable in real-world health care."

The team tested the device on 150 people, including patients in intensive care units and outpatient clinics. Unlike commercial wearables that use light to estimate blood pressure through a process whose scientific basis is not fully understood, the bioimpedance approach does not require calibration for individual users.

Multiple Approaches Converging

At UNC-Chapel Hill, a separate team led by assistant professor Wubin Bai developed a wearable using photoplethysmography (PPG) — the same light-based technology behind smartwatch heart rate sensors. Published in the IEEE Journal on Flexible Electronics, the study used two PPG sensors on a finger and a toe to measure pulse wave velocity, the time it takes blood to travel between two points.

Tested on 25 volunteers, the UNC device achieved accuracy within about 1 mmHg of a gold-standard reference device, meeting international accuracy guidelines for medical devices. It also tracked blood pressure changes during sleep, walking, biking, and typing.

Meanwhile, researchers at UC San Diego validated an ultrasound patch on 117 participants, including ICU patients and those in cardiac catheterization labs. Their patch delivered accuracy comparable to arterial lines — the invasive gold standard used in critical care — while remaining noninvasive and comfortable to wear.

Why It Matters for South Asian Health

Hypertension affects an estimated 1.28 billion adults worldwide, according to the World Health Organization, but the burden falls disproportionately on South Asian populations. Studies have consistently shown that people of South Asian descent develop hypertension at younger ages and at lower body weights compared to other ethnic groups, with higher rates of related complications including heart disease, stroke, and kidney failure.

Current monitoring relies on occasional cuff readings at doctor's visits — snapshots that miss the continuous fluctuations that drive cardiovascular risk. "Blood pressure isn't static. It changes all the time, influenced by stress, sleep, activity and diet," said Tien Nguyen, lead author of the UNC study. "A device that captures those fluctuations in real-world settings could help doctors make better treatment decisions and help patients take control of their health."

What's Next

The University of Utah holds the intellectual property for the bioimpedance technology and is exploring licensing opportunities. The UC San Diego team is developing a wireless, battery-powered version of its ultrasound patch and planning larger clinical trials. None of the devices are commercially available yet, but they represent a significant step toward making 24/7 blood pressure monitoring as routine as step counting.

"Our goal was to design something that's not only precise but also wearable in daily life," said Professor Bai. "If we can monitor blood pressure the way we track steps on a fitness watch, we could transform how we detect hypertension and prevent cardiovascular disease."
